ground_truth_root_cause: AWS EC2 instance-store physical hardware degradation on the database host (instanceId=i-0a3f7c9d2e1b4567, device=xvdb, physical host ph-use1-rack42-node07) caused catastrophic I/O degradation starting at 02:01:58Z. fsync latency escalated from under 4ms baseline to over 6000ms, driving disk await above 1000ms and utilization to 100%. This caused all MySQL writes and reads to stall, exhausting the DB connection pool with 100/100 connections blocked on fsync and cascading into frontend 503 errors. The degradation is entirely unrelated to any application or schema deploy.
ground_truth_remediation: 1. Immediately initiate an EC2 instance stop/start (NOT reboot) on i-0a3f7c9d2e1b4567 to migrate to a healthy physical host since instance-store I/O degradation requires host migration to resolve. 2. Promote a read replica from a different physical host as the new primary if stop/start takes more than 15 minutes. 3. Monitor xvdb await and fsync latency post-migration to confirm restoration to baseline under 5ms. 4. Open AWS support case referencing the instance-store health event on ph-use1-rack42-node07. 5. Consider migrating database storage to EBS io2 to eliminate instance-store reliability risk going forward.
red_herring: The database migration (SHA e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f4) deploying a composite index on orders(user_id, created_at) is highly suspicious: it ran approximately 75 minutes before the incident, it directly touches the orders table that appears in slow query logs, and composite indexes on large tables can cause query plan changes, lock contention, or I/O pressure during index builds. The slow query log even references USE INDEX idx_orders_user_created, the exact index created by this migration, making it tempting to blame the new index for a regression. However, the logs contain clear exculpatory evidence: (1) the migration-runner log at 02:03:25Z explicitly states the migration completed successfully at 01:44:32Z with 0 errors and replication lag post-migration of 0.3s which is normal, confirming no issues at migration time; (2) the db-host logs show kernel I/O errors on device xvdb and fsync latency spikes beginning at 02:02:22Z, fully 18 minutes after the migration completed cleanly with no anomalies; (3) the AWS EC2 instance-store degradation event is explicitly logged at 02:02:36Z and again at 02:03:35Z attributing the failure to physical host hardware; (4) the db-proxy log at 02:03:40Z explicitly states index scans are normal and the bottleneck is I/O wait not query plan, directly ruling out index-related slowness; (5) the I/O metrics show await rising from a 4ms baseline to 1341ms with IOPS collapsing from thousands to single digits, a pattern consistent only with storage hardware failure and not any application or schema change.
